title: Who Is the One Who Knows?
reflection: Once today, when a sharp I-statement arrives, such as I cannot cope, notice that the I in it is something you can be aware of. Do not argue with it. Just see whether it gives you a little room.

questions.q: When Kai looks at his cup, Swamiji finds three things in that single moment. What are they?
o: The cup, the seeing, and the one who sees it: a known, a knowing and a knower.
The cup, the table and the room: an object, its support and the space around it.
The eye, the brain and the mind: three organs working together to produce the view.
The light, the cup and the shadow: three physical facts that a camera could also record.
questions.e: Every act of the mind has the same shape: someone knowing something. It holds for a sound, a memory or a worry. James compares it to grammar, with subject, verb and object, and Swamiji calls it the grammar of experience.

questions.q: What do the words grāhya and grāhaka mean, in the lesson?
o: Grāhya is what is grasped, the thing known; grāhaka is the one who grasps, the knower.
Grāhya is the one who grasps, the knower; grāhaka is what is grasped, the thing known.
Grāhya is the body and grāhaka is the mind, taken together as the two halves of a person.
Grāhya is the past and grāhaka is the future, taken together as the two halves of time.
questions.e: The contemplative investigators of India named the two ends of every act of knowing. Swamiji adds that the words matter less than the observation: every act of knowing has two poles.
questions.c: Grāhya is the known; grāhaka is the knower

questions.q: Kai tries to point to the “you” who is looking at the cup and cannot find a spot. What does Swamiji say about this?
o: The known can be located but the knower is elusive: obvious, yet impossible to point at.
Kai has not looked hard enough, so with more effort he will find the knower behind his eyes and in his head.
The knower is in the head, so a brain scan could finally show where it is to be found in the body.
Nothing has been learned, since failing to find anything simply means that nobody is there at all.
questions.e: Kai says it feels totally obvious that he is here and totally impossible to point at. Swamiji calls this the first strange thing, and says Kai found it himself.
questions.c: The knower cannot be pointed at

questions.q: Sarah silently says “I am tired” and then notices the thought. What happens, and what follows from it?
o: The “I” becomes something she looks at, so whatever can be known is not, finally, the knower.
The “I” disappears for good, so Sarah has shown that she is no longer a person at all.
The “I” grows stronger, so the more she notices it the more she becomes tired and worn out.
The “I” is replaced by a thought, so the tiredness is shown to have been entirely imaginary.
questions.e: A moment ago “I am tired” was the subject; the instant she noticed it, the whole thing, including the I inside it, became an object. So the everyday I that seems in charge can itself be seen, and cannot be the deepest seer.
questions.c: The noticed I becomes an object

questions.q: “By noticing the watcher, then the one noticing the watcher, then the one noticing that, a person eventually catches the real watcher.”
questions.e: James tries it and finds it keeps going: every time he thinks he has caught the watcher, something behind it is doing the catching. Swamiji says that endless chain is the clue. Like the eye that cannot see itself, or the knife that cannot cut itself, the knowing is what does the looking.
questions.c: The chain never ends: the knowing cannot be caught

questions.q: “Swamiji is saying that Sarah does not exist, and that the lesson describes a special mystical state that has to be believed.”
questions.e: Swamiji says clearly that Sarah is completely real, with a body, a history and two children, and that none of that is denied. He is not describing a vision or a mystical state, and is not asking anyone to believe anything: it is careful looking, which each person can check.
questions.c: Nothing is denied and nothing is to be believed

questions.q: On a hard day, a young person thinks “I am a failure” and it feels like a verdict. What does the lesson offer?
o: See the everyday I appear within a wider awareness that is not itself anxious: space opens.
Argue the thought down, until the young person has proved that failure is not a fact about them at all.
Push the thought away, since the less attention it gets the sooner it will go out of mind altogether.
Accept the thought, since it is the final word about a person and no further space is to be found.
questions.e: Sarah finds that the noticing is quiet. The anxiety is still real, but it becomes one event in a much larger field instead of the entire sky. James adds that this is the child who can say I am noticing I feel panicky.

questions.q: A therapist teaches a patient to say “I am having the thought that I am a failure.” How does Swamiji connect this to the lesson?
o: It is the same space the group found: seeing thoughts as passing contents, not as the truth about who one is.
It is the opposite of what the group found: the patient must now believe the thought more firmly.
It is unrelated to the lesson, since therapy deals with feelings and the lesson deals with ideas.
It is a trick of words, which only works when a person has first been taught to ignore feelings.
questions.e: Mindfulness-based approaches, now used in clinics and hospitals, train people in exactly this move. Modern psychology arrived at it from the outside; the contemplatives of India mapped it from the inside.
questions.c: Mindfulness-based therapy makes the same move

questions.q: Kai says, “It is all the brain; awareness is just neurons firing.” How does Swamiji respond?
o: Brain research is valuable, but knowing which neurons fire in joy is not the joy as lived.
Brain research is false, so Kai should set it aside and rely only on what he can feel from within himself.
Brain research settles the matter, so the awareness is nothing more than the machinery that is seen in a scan.
Brain research is irrelevant, so no scientist has anything useful to say about joy, fear or awareness itself.
questions.e: Brain activity and lived knowing are not the same kind of thing. Swamiji says that keeping this distinction clear protects the science, since it stops two different questions from being mashed into one.
questions.c: Machinery is not the joy as lived

questions.q: In the practical experiment, a person watches a thought arrive. What does Swamiji ask them to do about the part that is aware of it?
o: Not to hunt for it, but to notice that noticing is happening and is not the thought.
To hunt for it until it is found, since that is how the experiment is meant to be completed.
To describe it in words afterwards, since the aim is to be able to explain it to other people.
To force it into view, since insight comes from effort and never from simply waiting for it.
questions.e: Swamiji says not to strain, because insight here never comes from forcing. The second half asks each person to catch a sharp I-statement, such as Sarah’s I am failing her, and see that the I is a content passing through, not the whole of them.
questions.c: Notice the noticing without hunting for it
